## What this changes

`iris_doc mode=put` stored a `[Type=INT]` routine as `.mac`, because `doc_name_with_suffix` tested
for `INC` and sent everything else to `.mac`, while `doc_name_from_source` (added by #530 in the
same file) read all three types correctly. One reader now serves both — `routine_suffix` — and the
put path resolves `[Type=INT]` per the rule settled on the issue thread, which is per-DOCUMENT and
not per-type:

| state of the namespace | answer |
|---|---|
| no `X.mac` | store the content as `X.int` — the INT-only legacy case the `routines` profile exists to serve |
| `X.mac` exists | REFUSE `INT_GENERATED_FROM_MAC`, write NOTHING, and name `X.mac` as the document to edit |
| the probe did not answer | REFUSE `INT_SIBLING_UNKNOWN`, write NOTHING, and carry WHY |

The third row is this repo's house rule, not an extra. A 401, a 5xx or a timeout on the sibling
probe has not discovered an absence; reading it as "there is no `X.mac`" stores an `.int` on a
measurement nobody took, and reading it as "a `.mac` is there" refuses on an equally invented fact.
It is its own outcome, carrying the reason.

Closes #537

## The premise, re-checked at HEAD before building

```
$ git grep -nE 'TYPE=INT|Type=INT' origin/master -- 'crates/**/*.rs'
doc.rs:344   // `[Type=INC]` is an include, `[Type=INT]` an intermediate; anything else is a .mac.
doc.rs:349   } else if flat.contains("TYPE=INT") {
tests/hook_document_name.rs:94  assert_eq!(name("ROUTINE OMORDL [Type=INT]\n"), "OMORD
title: fix(doc): store a [Type=INT] routine as .int, and refuse it where the .mac exists (#537)

body:
## The defect

`iris_debug(action=map_int)` read **every** frame as a CLASS frame. Measured on a live 2026.2
stack and reported in the issue thread:

```
iris_debug action=map_int error_string="<UNDEFINED>F2+1^OMCUSTL *X"
  -> ROUTINE_NOT_FOUND: "'OMCUSTL *X' is not a compiled class"
```

`parse_int_frame` handed `handle_iris_debug` a "class" name, the handler asked
`%Dictionary.CompiledClass` about it, got nothing — correctly, it is not a class — and answered
with a true sentence about a question nobody asked. In routine-based code that is the most common
frame of all. It is the house bug: a failed lookup served as a negative fact.

Three separate defects, each with its own assertions:

1. **the frame is never classified**, so a routine is looked up as a class;
2. **`strip_prefix('z')` was applied to routine labels.** For a class, `z` is the compiler's
   generated method-label prefix. In a routine, `zINIT^RTN` is a label the author typed and `INIT`
   need not exist at all;
3. **the routine name was not terminated.** IRIS appends the offending reference to an
   `<UNDEFINED>` frame, so ` *X` rode into the lookup. Fixing (1) alone would still have looked up
   `OMCUSTL *X`.

## The red I saw first

Written against `HEAD` before any implementation (full log kept; this is the whole result):

```
running 4 tests
test a_class_label_still_loses_its_z ... ok
test a_routine_label_keeps_its_z ... FAILED
test a_class_frames_trailing_detail_is_dropped_too ... FAILED
test the_offending
title: fix(534): classify an error frame before looking it up, and count LABEL+offset against .INT text

body:
Closes #533

## The defect

`iris_debug action=error_logs` answered `success: true, logs: []` on a path where
it had read nothing at all. A caller could not tell "the error log was read and is
empty" from "the read failed", and the two are completely different facts — one
means the namespace is healthy, the other means you are flying blind.

This is the repo's dominant bug shape: a failure answered as a negative fact.
Per CLAUDE.md the repair is a third outcome, not a nicer-looking empty one.

## The repair

A new `src/tools/error_log.rs` makes the outcome a total function over three
cases, so the ambiguity cannot be expressed:

| outcome | what the caller sees |
|---|---|
| `Entries { entries, total }` | the entries, plus the total, plus what was withheld under `limit` |
| `ReadAndEmpty` | `success: true`, **`log_read: true`**, `logs: []` |
| `Unreadable(why)` | `ERROR_LOG_UNAVAILABLE`, the reason, and **no `logs` key at all** |

The missing `logs` key in the third case is deliberate: an absent key cannot be
mistaken for an empty array by a caller that indexes before it checks.

The tests enumerate the ways a walk can fail and pin each one to `Unreadable`
rather than to empty — an empty reply, a truncated reply, an ObjectScript abort,
a partial entry, more entries than the stated total, a total above zero with no
entries, and an absent error table.

## Mutations

Each applied to the source, compiled, run, restored byte-identical, final suite
green (18 passed / 0 failed):

|
title: fix(debug): read the error log, and never answer an unread one as empty

body:
Closes #549

## The defect

`hook post-edit` took the file path from its event payload and applied exactly one
test to it — the extension — before reading it and uploading it into the namespace
named by `.iris-agentic-dev.toml`. A `PostToolUse` hook fires on whatever the agent
just edited, which is not always a file the project owns, so a scratch draft in a
temp directory or a file in another checkout was compiled into a namespace someone
else may be using.

This is the third time this hook has reported a verdict about something other than
what the agent edited: #529 the wrong VERSION, #540 the wrong NAMESPACE, this one
the wrong FILE. So the check lives in the library beside the other two as one total
function over three outcomes, and the binary's only job is to pick a channel.

## The fix

`path_within_project` canonicalises both sides, then compares path COMPONENTS via
`Path::starts_with`. Each half covers a distinct escape:

- **unresolved strings** — on macOS `/tmp` is a symlink to `/private/tmp`, so a path
  and a root naming the same directory through different links read as different
  trees, in either direction
- **a textual prefix** — `/a/project-other` begins with every character of
  `/a/project` and is not inside it

The third outcome is the point. A path or root that will not resolve is
`Undetermined`, never `Outside`: "I could not tell" and "it is outside" are
different facts, and collapsing them is this repo's commonest bug shape. An
unresolvable root is the d
title: fix(hook): bound post-edit compiles to the project root

> **This changes release infrastructure.** `.github/workflows/release.yml` gains two matrix rows on

## The defect, as opposed to the gap

#543 reports two things, and the second is the one that matters.

The gap: `release.yml` published Linux for x64 only, so an arm64 Linux host — Graviton, an arm64 CI
runner, Docker Desktop's arm64 Linux VM on an Apple-silicon Mac — had no asset it could execute.

The defect: the README's Linux install line named `iris-interop-dev-linux-x64` flatly, with no
`uname -m` anywhere, unlike the macOS line directly above it. So the arm64 host downloaded the x64
binary, the SHA-256 GitHub reports matched the bytes that arrived, and `exec` was the first thing
that failed. **A checksum that passes on a binary for another instruction set verified nothing.**

This is the third instance of one shape — #174 (GLIBC_2.39 floor) and #423 (macOS published arm64
only) both downloaded, hash-verified, and then died at exec. #423 added
`scripts/verify-asset-arch.sh`, which answers *"is this asset built for the architecture its NAME
promises"*. That runs at build time and cannot report an architecture for which no asset exists at
all, which
title: feat(release): publish Linux arm64, and refuse a wrong-arch download instead of verifying it

body:
The deletion flow, and the last of #532. `global_preview` lists exactly which nodes would go and
issues a token; `global_kill` spends it, re-checks that the subtree is still what was shown, and
only then removes it. `iris_global` has no kill action, so there is no path that deletes a global
without having listed it first.

## Why not a faithful port

Upstream has both tools. Three things it does that this does not, all read from its source:

1. **Its preview is depth-1.** `admin_tools.rs` generates a single `$Order` loop with a `$Get` per
   key, and its `total_subscripts` is incremented inside the loop under `If cnt>=limit Quit` — so
   with the default limit of 20 it maxes out at 20. A preview of a twenty-node subtree and of a
   million-node one are the same answer. The kill then removes the whole tree. Here the preview is
   the `walk` from #550: `$Query`, descending, reporting which bound stopped it.
2. **Its token binds `{global, server}`** — `entry.global != name || entry.server != params.server`
   — not the namespace, not the subscripts, not what was shown. The namespace is read separately
   from the live connection at each call, so the same token works in a different namespace.
3. **It has an untokened `iris_global action=kill` beside the token-requiring tool.** That split is
   the hole, not a convenience.

## The order the kill does things in

1. name validated, reserved families refused — no instance needed
2. token present, else `GLOBAL_CONFIRM_REQUIRED` naming
title: feat(global): delete a global only through the preview that showed it (#532)

`iris_global` gains one write action, `set`, and the system-global refusal that has to ship with it
rather than after it. Removal is deliberately **not** an action here — `global_preview` and
`global_kill` follow in the PR that completes issue 532, so there is exactly one destructive path and it is
the confirmed one.

## The premise in #532 was wrong, and that changed the design

#532 reads as "port the write half from upstream v1.6.2". Upstream already *has* a write half, and
I read it rather than inferring it: `crates/iris-agentic-dev-core/src/tools/global.rs` exists at
every tag — v1.2.6 (22,475 b), v1.6.2 (24,719 b), **v1.7.0 (29,946 b)** — with `"get"`/`"set"`/
`"kill"`/`"list"` arms. A 404 control on a neighbouring path confirms the API was not just echoing
successes.

Three things I found there changed what this PR does:

1. **v1.6.2 is not the version to port.** v1.7.0 replaces the `normalize` + `validate` pair with
   `canonical_global_name`, whose own doc comment calls it the fix for a caret bypass, and adds a
   128-char bound. Porting the version the issue names would ship a bug upstream has already fixed.
2. **Upstream's blocklist is bypassable exactly where it matters.** `system_blocklist_gate.rs:27-29`
   returns `None` — no refusal — *before* consulting the list when
   `is_kill_op && matches_any_owned(name, kill_allowlist)`, and that allowlist is the
   operator-settable config key `dataPolicyKillAllowlist`. The module doc says "Not bypassable by
   any confi
title: feat(iris_global): write one node, and refuse the globals IRIS owns (#532)

body:
`iris_global` reads a global in the `routines` profile: one node with its `$DATA` state, one
subscript level, or a bounded subtree walk. Write actions are not in this PR — see the scope note.

## What a caller gets

| action | answers |
|---|---|
| `get` | the node's `$DATA` code, its canonical `$NAME`, and its value — with "no value" and "the empty string" as different answers |
| `list` | one subscript level via `$Order`, resumable by subscript |
| `walk` | a `$Query` subtree bounded by node count *and* a wall clock, resumable by node |

Every bounded answer reports why it stopped: `done`, `cap` or `time`, read off the loop's own state
rather than inferred from how much came back. A walk that ran out of clock is not a complete walk,
and the payload says so in `complete` and `stopped_because`.

## Subscripts are data, not code

A subscript arrives as JSON and is rendered by `subscript_expr`: a JSON number goes out bare for
IRIS to canonicalise, a JSON string is **always** quoted through `os_str_expr`. So
`"ACME, INC."` is one subscript, a `"` inside one is doubled rather than closing the literal, a
`^` in one is data, and `") Kill ^IIDTest Set x=("` is a string that reads back as itself. A
non-canonic numeric string (`"01"`) stays a string subscript, because to IRIS it is one.

The global *name* is validated against a pattern before it is ever spliced, and an extended
reference (`^|"NS"|X`, `^["NS"]X`) is refused in those words — this tool reads the namespace it was
given, i
title: feat(iris_global): read globals in the routines profile — subscripts, $DATA and bounded walks (#532)

Two defects found on master `b117fdf` while testing the routines profile against a live stack,
both in surface this release introduces, both the house shape: a failure answered as a
plausible-but-wrong success. Together before the 0.26.0 tag because the tag is what the demo pins.

Found by the demo-ObjectScript session against its OMS stack. I verified both mechanisms here by

## 1. The hook compiled into the wrong namespace (#540)

`hook post-edit` took its **connection** from `.iris-agentic-dev.toml` and its **namespace** from

a second. The clap arg drops `env` and `default_value`: clap cannot tell `--namespace USER` from
the default, which is precisely why the hook could never know whether to defer. `IRIS_NAMESPACE`
keeps working, through connection resolution,

body:
Refs #531 — the code half. Part of #528.

`IRIS_TOOLSET=routines` / `--toolset routines`. The default stays `interop`, and the interop
profile is byte-for-byte unchanged.

## What the profile is

Legacy ObjectScript: `.mac` routines with dot syntax, `$PIECE`-delimited records in globals,
cross-reference globals, LOCK/TSTART. Three groups:

- **Shared with interop** — execution, compilation, testing, introspection. A routine is compiled
  and run the same way a class is.
- **Dropped** — production, rule, lookup, credential, HL7, gateway, interop query. A routine has no
  production to configure, and advertising those invites an agent to look for interop structure in
  code that has none.
- **Added** — `iris_search` and `iris_info`, both read-only, both excluded from interop on *scope*
  rather than merit (`tools-excluded.json` already marked them `wanted`). `iris_search` answers
  "which routine references this global", which a name-based search cannot.

So it is **neither a subset nor a superset of interop**. That is the intuition worth breaking, and
`test_routines_is_not_a_subset_of_interop` asserts both directions.

## The pruner change is the load-bearing one

It used to read `if toolset == Toolset::Interop`. It now asks `toolset.keep_list()`, so a
keep-list profile cannot be added without the pruner seeing it. The `else` branch it would
otherwise have fallen into prunes only the NOT_IMPLEMENTED stubs — which would have produced a
`routines` profile that advertised **every
title: feat(toolset): a `routines` profile for legacy ObjectScript (#531)

body:
Closes #529. Closes #530. Part of #528.

## The defect, in one line

The hook compiled a document name without ever uploading the file, and reported the verdict on a
channel the model does not read. It reported on a version the agent had not written, to nobody.

## What was wrong

`scripts/compile-hook.sh` is the `PostToolUse` hook on `Write|Edit` (plugin.json:33-39).

1. **It never uploaded.** One request only: `POST action/compile` with a document name
   (compile-hook.sh:53-58). No PUT anywhere in the file. IRIS compiled whatever copy it already
   held — the previous version, or nothing for a new document.
2. **Its verdict was unreadable.** Every path printed to stdout and exited 0 (lines 15, 20, 23, 27,
   60, 67, 81, 99 and the final echoes at 108/110). For `PostToolUse` that reaches the transcript
   view, not the model.
3. **#530: the name was built from the path** — one parent folder — so `src/OM/API/Customer.cls`
   was sent as `API.Customer.cls`, and the resulting 404 was reported as a namespace problem.

## What it does now

`iris-interop-dev hook post-edit` reads the hook payload on stdin. It PUTs the source, **waits for
that to succeed**, and only then compiles — so a verdict is always about the bytes on disk.

| outcome | exit | channel |
|---|---|---|
| compiled clean | 0 | one line of `additionalContext`, naming the document |
| compile errors | 2 | stderr — the one channel the model re

body:
Closes #465.

## The leak

`execute_via_generator_once` PUTs `IrisDevTmp.Run<id>`, compiles it, and only then runs
`SELECT <proc>() AS result`. Four call sites wrap the whole thing in `tokio::time::timeout`
(`tools/mod.rs`: iris_test twice, iris_coverage, iris_execute), so an elapsed timeout drops
the future **after** the PUT and the compile have succeeded. No DELETE is ever sent and a
compiled class stays in the namespace. The three `?` returns after the PUT — the compile
send, the query send, the body read — leak by the same route: an early return is a drop.

Measured before the fix, against a mock counting requests:

```
a_timeout_that_drops_the_generator_still_deletes_the_scratch_class ... FAILED
  left: 0   right: 1     # zero DELETEs
```

Upstream found 78,183 leaked classes in one namespace. 15 `IrisDevTmp.%` classes were sitting
in namespace APP on the local instance when #465 was triaged (control: the same query shape
counted 463 `Ens.%`, so a zero would have been readable as real).

## The fix is in `Drop`, not at the timeouts

A `ScratchGuard` is armed immediately after the PUT succeeds and covers all four exits with
**none of the call sites changing** — that is the whole reason for putting it in `Drop`. `Drop`
is synchronous and this crate builds reqwest without the `blocking` feature, so the DELETE goes
out on the ambient runtime when there is one (the timeout case, where the runtime outlives the
dropped future) and on a thread with its own when there is none.

#
title: fix(generator): the scratch class is deleted when the future is dropped (#465)

## What

Two comments name the reader of the generator's response shape, and both called it
`row_count`. No function by that name exists in the tree. The reader is
`get_row_count`, at `crates/iris-agentic-dev-core/src/tools/info.rs:1330`.

- `src/tools/mod.rs:2998` — the doc comment on `no_rows()`
- `src/tools/mod.rs:4093` — inside `declared_members`

## Why the wrong name reads as plausible

`row_count` is real, just not as a function: it is the JSON key `get_row_count`
writes (`obj["row_count"]`, info.rs:1252/1281) and the SQL alias it reads back
(`SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count`, info.rs:1347). So the comment names a true string
in a false role — a reader who greps `fn row_count` gets zero hits and has no way to
tell a renamed function from a mis-named one.

## Measured

```
$ git grep -c 'fn row_count' -- crates          # 0
$ git grep -n 'fn get_row_count' -- crates      # info.rs:1330 (+ the guard test)
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check                    # exit 0
```

The `fn row_count` zero is controlled: the same sweep for `fn get_row_count` returns
hits, so the pattern style finds functions when they exist.

Nothing greps either comment phrase — checked before rewording, since text someone
greps is an undeclared contract in this repo. `tests/row_count_is_a_read.rs` keys on
`async fn get_row_count(` and `AS row_count` in `info.rs`, neither of which this
touches.

Comments only: no behaviour change, no test change, no new assertion. This does not
address #303

body:
Closes #523.

`execute_via_generator` step 3 read the captured output as
`content[0]["result"].as_str().unwrap_or("")`. #362 separated the three reply shapes that carry
something to **report** — an IRIS error in `status.errors`, a non-2xx status, a non-JSON body. The
shape that carries **nothing** was still defaulting to the empty string, and an empty string from
this function is what call sites read as *the script produced no output*.

## Measured, which is why this is a third case and not a defensive invention

`POST /api/atelier/v8/<ns>/action/query` on a live instance:

| query | HTTP | `status.errors` | `result.content` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SELECT 1 AS result WHERE 1=0` | 200 | `[]` | `[]` |
| `SELECT Name AS result FROM %Dictionary.ClassDefinition WHERE Name = 'ZZ.Nope'` | 200 | `[]` | `[]` |
| `SELECT NULL AS result` | 200 | `[]` | `[{"result": ""}]` |
| `SELECT NoSuchFunc() AS result` | 200 | SQLCODE -359 | — |

`interpret_query_response` classifies rows 1–2 as `Rows` (success, no errors), `content[0]` is then
`null`, and `unwrap_or("")` reports it as an empty output.

**Row 3 is the half that makes the split safe**, and it is why `captured_output` keys on the ROW
rather than on the value: a SQL NULL arrives as the empty **string**, not as JSON null, so a row
that is present always carries something `as_str()` can read. The legitimate "script wrote nothing"
path therefore cannot be caught by the new case — `a_script_that_writes_nothing_still_succeeds_with_an_empty_o
title: fix(generator): a reply that carried no row is not an empty output (#523)

body:
## What

`iris_production_item(action=get_settings)` returned each setting as `Name=Value` and dropped `Ens.Config.Setting.Target`. `set_settings` distinguishes the two targets by key prefix (`Adapter.FilePath` → adapter, bare key → Host, via `resolve_setting_target`), so the output of a read could not be fed back into a write for **any** adapter setting — measured at 23 of 65 settings on a real production, and nothing in the response said which.

The generated program now writes `Target:Name=Value`, and the map key is rendered as the exact inverse of `resolve_setting_target`.

A `:`-delimited **first** field is safe where `=` is not: Target is a short closed token, whereas the real `ReplyCodeActions` value is `:?R=F,:?E=F,:~=S,…`, which is precisely why the parser already splits on `=` with `splitn(2, …)`. The split stays in Rust rather than being pre-prefixed in ObjectScript, keeping #212's single-place rule.

## Prefixing is total, not adapter-only

This is the part that matters, and it is not what the issue originally proposed. `interop.rs:2786` records that the pre-#212 bug actually created, in the field, a **Host** setting literally named `Adapter.DSN`. Emitted bare, that key reads back as target=`Adapter`, name=`DSN` — a silent **move** of the setting.

So a Host key is qualified (`Host.Adapter.DSN`) if and only if its own name already begins `Adapter.` or `Host.`; otherwise it is emitted unchanged. That keeps **42 of the 65** measured keys byte-identical while making

## What

One causal chain, fixed at both ends. These are one PR because #391's fix touches the exact lines #390's fix rewrites.

**The chain.** `execute_via_generator_once` step 2 decided "did the scratch class compile?" from `result.log` alone and never consulted `status.errors` — so a whole class of compile failures (`ERROR #5559`, which one stray brace produces) was invisible, and the error that eventually surfaced named the **SqlProc** rather than the brace. `iris_execute` then could not tell "the transport failed" from "IRIS ran the code and reported an error", so it routed that into the docker-exec fallback and answered `DOCKER_REQUIRED` — advising the caller to fix Docker when HTTP had answered 200.

It was worse than #390 reported: `mod.rs:7034` did not interpolate the HTTP leg's error at all, so the IRIS text was **dropped outright**.

### #391 — record at step 2, surface at step 3

Step 2 no longer branches. It records the verdict through the shared `compile_error_list` (now reading `status.errors` ∪ `result.log` ∪ console, so all four compile-verdict consumers read the same union), and step 3 surfaces it where whether `Execute()` ran is the authoritative test.

**Deliberately not a step-2 bail.** The issue author implemented that, drove it through the shipped binary and measured a regression: `Set x=` went from a good answer (`IRIS_RUNTIME_ERROR`, `<SYNTAX>`, `source_line`) to a bare failure, because with `flags=cuk` a class can carry a reported compile error and s

## What

Three things, in the order they have to land:

1. **A live leak, repaired.** `undriveable_refusal` (`scm.rs:636`, `:642`) carried **three 18-space runs** in two refusal messages. They reach clients through `err_json` at `scm.rs:944`/`:1023` and through `Precheck::Refuse` in `iris_doc` (`doc.rs:1192`). Measured before: internal runs at offsets 93 and 189 on line 636 and offset 97 on line 642. After: `internal runs found: 0`. Same codes, same wording, same `{where_}` suffix — only the continuations are re-split.

   This landed on **2026-10-06, one day after #376/#377 fixed the original seven**, so the class recurred immediately and no test saw it.

2. **The producer assertion it never had.** `undriveable_refusal` and `CodeMeaning` are `pub(crate)`, so this test lives in `scm.rs`'s own `#[cfg(test)]` mod. It iterates **all 256 `u8` codes** through `CodeMeaning::of` rather than a hand-written variant list, because every call site reaches the function as `undriveable_refusal(CodeMeaning::of(action_code), …)` — so the domain really is 0..=255 and the population needs no roster kept in step.

   The earlier draft of this test walked a six-entry array and derived its `checked == 12` control *from that same array*, so a variant that existed but was not listed was invisible to both the check and its control. The `match` tripwire covered the `match`, not the population.

3. **The gate.** A new integration test reconstructs each non-raw string literal **as the compiler would**

§5 and §6's gate in #421.

## §1's residue: the answer is a labelled record, found wherever the hook put it

#422 read the action code from the first line. That is still wrong when the hook writes first, which
CCR does: a `NOTICE:` line when no Perforce user is defined, a `CMD: p4 …` echo whenever it shells
out. The issue proposes a delimited record — `$c(1)_"IAD|"_action_"|"_target_$c(1)`.

```text
  ->  "IADSCM|{\"msg\":\"line one\\nline two\"}\n"        lines = 1
```

`SCMSTATUS|…` line and finds it among noise, and `status` is the one arm §1 did not list as

promises" a thing that is checked rather than assumed.

## The gap

Every platform this workflow builds for was already x64 **except macOS**, which was published for
arm64 only:

| asset | target | before |
|---|---|---|
| `iris-interop-dev-windows-x64.exe` | `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` | x64 ✓ |
| `iris-interop-dev-linux-x64` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` | x64 ✓ |
| `iris-interop-dev-linux-x64-musl` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` | x64 ✓ |
| `iris-interop-dev-macos-arm64` | `aarch64-apple-darwin` | arm64 only |
| **`iris-interop-dev-macos-x64`** | **`x86_64-apple-darwin`** | **absent** |

An Intel Mac had no asset, and the failure is not a 404 — the arm64 file downloads, hash-verifies,
and dies at exec. That reads as a broken release rather than a missing build, which is exactly #174's
shape with the instruction set as the floor instead of GLIBC.

Built on an **Intel runner** rather than cross-compiled from arm64, so the existing `--version`
provenance guard still executes the artifact it is vouching for. Cross-compiling would have meant
installing Rosetta on the runner purely so that guard could run, or skipping it for the one asset
whose architecture is least verifiable.

Closes #417

Advertises `iris_source_control` in the interop profile, write-gated action by action. This is #417's
first checkbox and #418's item 6, and they cannot be split — see below.

## Why one change

`every_interop_tool_is_classified` asserts that every `INTEROP_TOOLS` entry appears in
`mutating_call`'s explicit arms. Adding the keep-list entry alone does not compile-and-pass, it goes
red. That coupling is the point: this tool can `%CheckIn`, `%GetLatest` and `%Disconnect`, and
shipping it in the **default** profile without the gate would run those on a connection the caller
asked to be read-only. #418 names `%Disconnect` specifically as reachable today with nothing in
front of it.

## The classification

A tool-level verdict is wrong in both directions. Blanket-mutating refuses `status` and `menu`,
which are the read path that makes the tool worth having on a read-only connection; blanket-read
ships the writes ungated. So the gate is action-aware, and it **derives** from a new
`ScmAction::is_write` rather than restating the action ids:

| action | verdict | why |
|---|---|---|
| `status`, `menu` | read | query the hook's state; nothing moves |
| `checkout` | **write** | takes a lock in the SCM |
| `execute` | per `action_id`, via `ScmAction::is_write` | |
| `execute` with an unknown or missing `action_id` | **write** | parses to `Unknown`, see below |
| any unrecognised top-level action | **write** | the gate must not be what assumes it is harmless |

Master's `test` job is failing at `78f51b3` and `68c7580`:

```
error: unused variable: `not_found`   crates/iris-agentic-dev-core/src/tools/interop.rs:2895
error: unused variable: `prologue`    crates/iris-agentic-dev-core/src/tools/interop.rs:2898
error: could not compile `iris-agentic-dev-core` (lib) due to 2 previous errors
```

`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` turns both into errors, so the job exits 101. `e2e-tests`, `benchmark-lint`, `windows-handshake` and `cross-compile-check` all passed on the same commit — this is the whole failure.

## Why both PRs were green and the merge is not

`not_found` and `prologue` were bound once in `interop_production_item_impl` and consumed by two arms:

| arm | consumer before | consumer after |
|---|---|---|
